articles.title: A 7,000-square-foot vacant California lot has become a community refuge where residents can cool off during heat waves, charge phones during blackouts, and prepare for disasters
articles.summary: US News: San Ysidro, the busiest border crossing in the United States, now has a haven for residents vulnerable to climate change. Casa Familiar, an environmen.
articles.body: San Ysidro, the busiest border crossing in the United States, now has a haven for residents vulnerable to climate change. Casa Familiar, an environmental justice nonprofit, officially opened La Semilla Community Resiliency Center this week on a once-vacant 7,000-square-foot lot, according to a report by KPBS. The centre, which sits on West Park Avenue near Hall Avenue, was inaugurated on Thursday, September 3.Residents of San Ysidro now have a place to cool down during heat waves, charge their devices during blackouts, and gather when disasters strike.First-of-its-kind climate resiliency centreLa Semilla Community Resiliency Center is a first-of-its-kind project in the San Diego area. Think of it as a haven for those vulnerable to climate change. Lisa Cuestas, CEO of Casa Familiar, the nonprofit organisation that built the centre, said it is a place where residents learn to prepare for extreme weather and other climate threats.“This hub is absolutely an education space on how to react and how to respond and how to get ready for disasters and emergencies,” she said during the ribbon-cutting ceremony. The organisation plans to host a community workshop on September 23 focused on preparing residents for an intensifying El Niño winter.“Our climate is changing. We see it all around us, and this is one of the ways we’re trying to address it,” Mayor Todd Gloria said at the ceremony."In 2024, we broke ground on La Semilla – a vacant lot with a vision to become something much more for the community. Today, that vision is a resource center designed to help residents in San Ysidro and beyond prepare for the climate challenges we’re already facing. This is what investment in San Ysidro looks like: transforming vacant spaces into resources that strengthen neighborhoods, build climate resilience, and prepare San Diegans for the future. What started as a seed is now taking root, and I’m excited to see how La Semilla continues to grow," he added.Building green to beat pollutionThe centre itself is built with a climate-smart approach. The main building was built using mass timber, large wood panels that store carbon. They carry a smaller carbon footprint than steel and concrete, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute. Even on a dark day, the centre won’t go dark, as solar panels generate power. Electric vehicle charging stations are also available at the centre. A community garden grows food. Water cisterns capture and store rainfall.Bertha Ruiz, who has lived in San Ysidro for 30 years, helped guide the centre’s design. During the ceremony, she said that she realised how polluted San Ysidro truly was only after respiratory problems plagued her family.San Ysidro has been subjected to more environmental challenges than most neighbourhoods. About 100,000 vehicles cross the U.S.-Mexico Port of Entry daily. In 2024, the San Ysidro crossing handled roughly 15 million cars entering the United States, according to the Federal Highway Administration. This is more than any other port of entry shared with Mexico. All those vehicles idling in border queues release exhaust directly into residential blocks. But that is not the only problem San Ysidro residents face. The Tijuana River, which carries sewage pollution across the border, has contributed to high hydrogen sulphide levels that repeatedly exceed state standards. The freeways cutting through the neighbourhood add another layer of air quality degradation.Ruiz added that La Semilla is bringing nature and more mobility options to her neighbourhood.This project was made possible with an $8.5 million grant from the California Strategic Growth Council, Cuestas added.While the centre is a haven in the face of climate challenges, it is more than a cooling space. The residents are learning skills and strategies for reducing energy use, managing extreme heat, and preparing for emergencies. The project is positioned in a community that faces significant challenges like air quality, clean transportation, sustainable living spaces, water and energy conservation. In a climate-disrupted future, that’s the kind of hope worth building on.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: As the China-US AI race reaches Cairo, Egypt faces a strategic decision
articles.summary: Egypt walks a tightrope as China and the US vie for dominance in AI data centre development.
articles.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s three-day visit to Egypt, coinciding with the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two nations, marked his first trip to the Middle East in four years and the first to Egypt in a decade.

The trip caused debate among geopolitical observers over Egypt’s diplomatic balancing act between China, one of its largest economic partners, and the United States, a major defence and strategic partner.

But Egypt also finds itself in another tightrope walk between the two superpowers: it is emerging as a potential battleground in the US-China artificial intelligence race.

Xi’s visit came at a time when Chinese tech giant Huawei has submitted a tender to build Egypt’s AI data centres. The US, meanwhile, is reportedly pulling together an offer to counter Huawei’s bid. Whoever wins the contract to build the data centres will also gain an opportunity to strengthen their political and economic ties with Egypt.

Egypt, which receives roughly $1.3bn a year in US military aid and remains a major American defence partner, has been steadily deepening its economic and military ties with China in recent years.

So what does all of this mean for Egypt’s relations with the US and China, and who stands to benefit from AI data centres in Egypt?

Huawei has offered to supply “1,408 Ascend 950 processors for AI model training, plus 600 Ascend 950 or older 910B chips” to build two computing clusters.

The company proposed a 12-month build timeline, and if the project goes through, the deal would mark the first known export of Huawei’s Ascend AI processors, according to documents reviewed by Bloomberg. The infrastructure that would house the AI chips would be used for military, surveillance and other public-sector operations, the news agency reported.

According to anonymous sources quoted by Bloomberg, the US State Department is working on a counteroffer to Huawei’s AI chip bid through companies including Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices Inc, and Microsoft Corp.

Currently, China and the United States are leading globally when it comes to AI development and investment. The gap between the world’s two biggest economies is narrowing fast, though. On spending alone, the US still dominates, with American firms pouring $285.9bn into private AI investment in 2025, against China’s $12.4bn, according to the 2026 AI Index Report by Stanford University.

Al Jazeera contacted Huawei for comment but received no response.

“The US and China are globally competing over data centres”, human rights advocate from the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), Mohamed Ramadan, tells Al Jazeera. “The question of data centres is a very significant geopolitical one”, he added.

“This competition primarily revolves around data and the ability of both nations to integrate data from different regions worldwide, which is essentially a battle over the future in some way.”

Ramadan, however, argued that China might have an advantage over the US in Egypt as “Huawei has been in Egypt for years” having signed numerous agreements with the Egyptian government for the supply of telecom equipment. He also added that the “Chinese often likely have the advantage of being cheaper compared to American companies.”

Environmentally, Egypt sits at a disadvantage when it comes to water scarcity and air pollution. The country’s per capita water share has fallen below 500 cubic metres a year, under half the UN’s water poverty threshold, according to Egyptian government data.

Data centres are notoriously water and power-hungry because high processing power requires significant cooling. Egypt’s capital is also ranked among the world’s most polluted cities, raising the question of whether an AI data centre could make the situation more severe.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Egyptian political analyst Maged Mandour said that despite water scarcity being a prominent issue, the government will likely supply the project “the water that it requires, and the energy that it needs while depriving other parts of the country of the needed resources”.

He added that the deal would be “an export deal of AI technologies” and would not necessarily benefit the Egyptian economy.

“I think it’s unlikely to lead to sustained employment … maybe it would create some jobs, but it’s not something that would be economically transformative long-term in general in a large country like Egypt.”

Why did China choose Egypt for an AI data centre?

The reason lies in where Egypt sits on the map. The country controls the Suez Canal, and it sits at the crossroads of Africa, the Middle East, Europe and Asia, making it both a sizeable market for Chinese companies and a potential manufacturing and logistics hub for reaching everyone around it.

Against a backdrop of regional conflict, driven by the six-month US-Israel war on Iran, and the partial closure and restriction of the vital waterway, the Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal’s strategic significance has only grown. It is today an obvious choice for an alternative shipping route. Routing through the Suez Canal sidesteps both the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb straits, letting cargoes avoid any potential risks that could be faced there.

China is Egypt’s largest trading partner in non-petroleum goods, with bilateral trade reaching nearly $20.7bn by the end of 2025, according to the State Information Service (SIS).

Egypt is also an important economic partner for China. The North African country imported $10bn of Chinese goods in the first half of this year alone, according to Egyptian government data, up more than 14 percent from the same period a year earlier.

Chinese investment has surged since Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi signed a strategic partnership agreement in Beijing in 2014. Since then, Chinese firms have poured billions into different Egyptian projects ranging from container ports, green hydrogen and factories producing iron pipes, car tyres and satellites.

According to figures cited by China’s Xinhua news agency, the China-Egypt Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone attracted more than 200 companies and created more than 10,000 direct jobs by the end of June. That zone is a major international industrial and manufacturing hub located along Egypt’s Red Sea coast and was established as a joint project between China and Egypt as part of China’s Belt and Road Initiative.

articles.title: Why Putin’s first visit to disputed Kuril Islands has rattled Japan
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Vladimir Putin first became Russia’s president in 2000 and has remained in power ever since, apart from a four-year stint as prime minister under Dmit.
articles.body: Vladimir Putin first became Russia’s president in 2000 and has remained in power ever since, apart from a four-year stint as prime minister under Dmitry Medvedev from 2008 to 2012.Yet Putin only travelled to the Kuril Islands, a Russian-controlled Pacific archipelago also claimed by Japan, for the first time in August this year. His visit predictably triggered a diplomatic spat between Moscow and Tokyo, reigniting a decades-long territorial dispute.The timing of the visit was also notable: he arrived just two days before the 81st anniversary of Japan’s surrender in World War II.However, the significance of Putin’s trip goes beyond it being his first to the Kurils or its timing, bringing renewed attention to a territorial dispute that has long complicated relations between Moscow and Tokyo.Putin’s Kuril Islands visit — A territorial dispute reignitedThe dispute centres on four of the 56 islands that make up the Kuril Islands, a volcanic archipelago stretching between Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula and Japan’s Hokkaido. The four are the southernmost islands in the chain and, therefore, the closest to Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories. Moscow, on the other hand, claims and administers them as Southern Kurils.On August 13, Putin went to Iturup, known as Etorofu in Japan, the largest of the four disputed islands. But he was not the first Russian leader to visit Southern Kurils. In 2010, Medvedev visited the islands as president and returned three times as prime minister, in 2012, 2015 and 2019. Mikhail Mishustin, Russia’s prime minister since 2020, also travelled to the Iturup island in 2021.Putin's visit also marked a departure from the approach he had taken toward the dispute for much of the 2010s, when he held multiple rounds of talks with then-Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe.In 2018, Putin even proposed signing a peace treaty “without any preconditions” to formally end their hostlities from World War II.Abe welcomed the proposal while acknowledging the difficulties ahead, saying, “We are both fully aware that it will not be easy.”However, that potential opening ultimately collapsed in 2022, when Russia withdrew from negotiations.Ukraine further strains an already tense relationshipOn February 24, 2022, Russia launched what it calls a “special military operation” against neighbouring Ukraine. More than four years later, the war continues, with no end in sight.The West responded by imposing sanctions on Russia and has added further measures since then. Japan also imposed sanctions, including on Putin himself. Moscow retaliated by suspending an exchange programme and withdrawing from dialogue on joint economic activities, both involving the disputed territories.It also withdrew from negotiations on a formal peace treaty, leaving the two countries without an agreement formally ending their World War II hostilities.For the Kremlin, Japan’s alignment with the West marked a sharp break from the relationship Putin had spent years trying to cultivate with Tokyo, particularly under Abe.The dispute, once the subject of sustained bilateral negotiations, was now caught up in the much wider confrontation between Russia and the West. In February 2026, the Kremlin declared that there would be “no dialogue” with Japan on a peace agreement, blaming what it described as Tokyo’s “unfriendly” stance.Russia's relations with Japan have been reduced to zero over Tokyo's unfriendly stance... There is no dialogue, and it is impossible to discuss the issue of a peace treaty without dialogueA message to more assertive Japan?Putin’s visit to Iturup coincided with another significant development. On August 21, Russia announced that its Navy had conducted a rare missile test near Southern Kurils, drawing another protest from Tokyo.That test, while not specifically aimed at Japan, came amid a significant shift in Tokyo’s security policy. Since becoming prime minister in October last year, Sanae Takaichi has pursued a more assertive security policy, marking a departure from Japan’s traditionally pacifist postwar posture.Much of that shift has focused on the potential threats posed by China and North Korea. But Takaichi has also been sharply critical of Moscow, which has grown closer to both Beijing and Pyongyang.Her response to Putin’s Iturup visit reflected that harder line. She described the trip as "absolutely unacceptable" and “incompatible with the Japanese position on the Northern Territories," and warned that restoring bilateral ties had become more difficult.Why Southern Kurils matter to RussiaWhile Southern Kurils has its own strategic importance for Japan, they are equally significant to Russia.The chain separates the Sea of Okhotsk from the Pacific Ocean, giving Moscow control over strategically important sea routes and helping protect the area where the Russian Navy’s Pacific Fleet operates.Beyond their strategic value, the islands are surrounded by rich fishing grounds. Before relations sharply deteriorated following the Ukraine war, Moscow and Tokyo had the 1998 Russia-Japan Fisheries Agreement, which allowed Japanese fishermen to operate in the region in return for payments to Moscow.Russia suspended the agreement in June 2022, months after the Ukraine war began, although it cited continued non-payment by Japan as the reason.Beyond Russia’s military presence on the disputed territory, the islands are home to around 20,000–30,000 inhabitants. There is also a civilian Russian presence, with settlements, schools, hospitals and other infrastructure spread across the inhabited islands.Putin’s itinerary on Iturup offered a glimpse of that presence. He toured a fish-processing plant, a hospital and a school, and met local officials and residents.The trip, therefore, also highlighted the civilian population and infrastructure Russia has built on the islands over the past eight decades.Signficance of Putin's Kuril Islands visitThe first time a Russian president toured Southern Kurils, with Medvedev visiting in 2010, Japan responded by recalling its ambassador from Moscow. Since his three subsequent trips were less high-profile, Tokyo limited its response to lodging diplomatic protests and summoning Russian ambassadors.According to experts, Putin’s decision to make the trip himself, therefore, carries a different significance. While Tokyo has protested and reportedly even considered recalling its ambassador from Moscow, it has so far taken no action beyond that.Putin's visit can also be seen as a reflection of the changed relationship between Russia and Japan. Rather than approaching the territory as an issue to be resolved through diplomacy, he made it a point to travel there, where he spent time touring local facilities and meeting residents.The timing also stood out. The four disputed islands were seized by the Soviet Union at the end of the war, making the timing difficult to separate from the history at the heart of the dispute.Taken together, this suggests that the visit was not simply a routine trip to territory Russia controls — and claims. It came when diplomacy with Japan has largely stalled, tensions have risen and Moscow has become more willing to publicly demonstrate its control over the islands.Kuril Islands: A dispute that enduresThe episode, therefore, highlights a stark geopolitical reality: the decades-long dispute is unlikely to be resolved anytime soon.More than 80 years later, Southern Kurils remain under Russian control and are still claimed by Japan. The disagreement has persisted despite changes in leadership, repeated rounds of negotiations and, now, a major deterioration in bilateral ties.Putin’s trip did not resolve any of those differences. Instead, it highlighted how much the context around them has changed. The president who once proposed ending the two countries’ World War II hostilities “without any preconditions” has now personally visited territory that Tokyo continues to regard as its own.For now, there is little sign that the issue that once brought Putin and the now-deceased Abe to the negotiating table is heading towards another diplomatic opening.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘No free cake’: Vancouver bakery owner calls out NBA star’s family over collaboration request, asks how an NBA legend can't afford a birthday cake for his kid
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Vancouver bakery owner has refused to give away a custom birthday cake for free after receiving a request from an assistant representing former NBA .
articles.body: A Vancouver bakery owner has refused to give away a custom birthday cake for free after receiving a request from an assistant representing former NBA star Metta Sandiford-Artest’s family, saying that social-media publicity does not cover the costs of running a small business.Fanny Lam, owner of Oh Sweet Day! Bake Shop, said she was approached by an individual identifying themselves as an assistant to Sandiford-Artest and his wife, Maya. The request was for a custom cake for their son’s birthday celebration in Richmond, British Columbia.'We felt particularly frustrated because of the imbalance'The proposed arrangement was a familiar one in the age of influencer marketing: the bakery would provide the cake at no cost, while the family would promote the business through social media posts and Instagram stories.Lam, however, was not convinced that the exposure was worth the price of the cake.The custom order could have cost around C$200 to C$300, depending on its size and design. For a small bakery, Lam said, that represents real costs in ingredients, labour and preparation time.“We felt particularly frustrated because of the imbalance,” Lam told CTV News. “A small business like us being asked to custom make something out of pocket for somebody who is considerably more financially successful to take it for free.”‘Publicity doesn’t pay the bills’Lam said she receives such requests regularly and generally does not agree to them. While social-media promotion can potentially help a business attract customers, she believes it should not automatically be treated as equivalent to payment.The issue, she said, is particularly stark when the request comes from people who can afford to pay for the product themselves.Sandiford-Artest, formerly known as Metta World Peace and Ron Artest, spent 17 seasons in the NBA. He was part of the Los Angeles Lakers team that won the NBA championship in 2010.Lam shared the 'collaboration' email on social media. The proposal said that Metta and Maya will be celebrating their son Hiro's 2nd birthday with a "Calling All Party Animals" farm-themed party in Richmond. "I am reaching out to a select few local vendors of their choosing that they'd love to feature as part of the day. The family has a strong social media following and will be sharing the celebration across their platforms, including posts/stories crediting and tagging vendors involved," the email said.Lam said after she posted it on social media, the NBA star's team reached out to her but not to apologize but asking to remove the post as the assistant emailed. Lam said she hid the party information after their request."You cannot tell me that an NBA legend can’t afford a birthday cake for his kid, and asks a small bakery making approximately 0.0001% of his fortune for a free cake," Lam said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US envoys headed to Russia and Ukraine to relaunch mediation
articles.summary: Amid hopes for diplomacy, a Russian strike hits the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU security service in Kyiv.
articles.body:
United States envoys are expected to arrive in Kyiv and Moscow over the weekend, in an apparent bid to revive negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war on Ukraine .

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said late on Thursday that US negotiators were set for meetings in both capitals “in the coming days” and that Ukraine is ready for substantive, high-level negotiations.

Russia’s state news agency TASS reported on Friday that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would be in Moscow on September 5 and 6.

President Donald Trump’s envoys were most recently in the Russian capital in January. However, Washington’s mediation efforts have all but halted since the US and Israel launched war on Iran in March.

The talks come as both sides continue to exchange attacks, with Russia hitting the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU security services on Friday.

Zelenskyy was enthusiastic in announcing the return of US-backed talks, despite Washington having previously been accused of adopting Russian narratives and demands for ending the war, primarily that Kyiv should hand over territory.

The Ukrainian president said in a late-night address on Thursday that his country’s negotiating team is in near-constant contact with the US side and preparing for talks.

“They confirmed they will have a meeting in Moscow and another one in Kyiv. We expect the latter to take place in the coming days. This is very important. It is important that America remain actively engaged,” he said, adding that Ukraine is ready for substantive, high-level negotiations.

The TASS report said Witkoff and Kushner – respectively, Trump’s real estate partner and son-in-law – will first arrive in Moscow. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov refused to confirm reports at a later news briefing.

However, with talks evidently taking place in the background, officials on both sides of the conflict appear to have new hope of progress towards a settlement.

Following Kushner and Witkoff’s last visit to Moscow, Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov described talks as constructive, but said that “reaching a long-term settlement can’t be expected without solving the territorial issue”.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had said recently that negotiations were “frozen”.

However, speaking at an economic forum in Russia’s Far East on Thursday, he said that a number of countries, including the US and China, are ready to support a peace deal, and hinted at possible progress.

“We are grateful to everyone attempting ⁠to contribute to a settlement,” he said, according to the Reuters news agency. “Is there a chance? In my view, yes, there is.”

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha earlier told reporters in Kyiv that he saw a “new dynamic” ⁠coming in peace efforts, with more active political and diplomatic engagement.

However, in the eight months since Witkoff and Kushner were last in Moscow, Russia and Ukraine have ramped up air attacks deep inside the other’s territory and at sea, as well as the fighting along the front line in eastern Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said on Friday that a Russian drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU security services in central Kyiv.

At least five people were wounded in the strike, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Foreign Minister Sybiha condemned the attack, saying it was “a major escalation that demands resolute responses.”

In a post on social media, Sybiha said “Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace – laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy.”

Al Jazeera’s Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said that while people weren’t shocked the SBU building was hit, it has made them wonder what target might be next.

“It’s not so much that people never expected the SBU to be hit, but it really raises the question of if Russia can hit this, what else can it hit?”, she said, adding that the question today on everyone’s mind is “about just how much things will escalate”.

“Some people here are wondering whether this attack, for example, could be aimed at possibly dissuading” the US envoys’ trips to Ukraine, said Macalpine.

Moscow’s forces have relentlessly struck civilian areas over the four and a half years since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Kyv mayor Klitschko said at least nine people, seven of which are medical personnel, were injured in a Russian drone attack on the capital’s Shevchenkivskyi district on Friday.

A “massive” overnight Russian attack on the southern Odesa region also killed one person and injured at least five others, including a child, regional head Oleh Kiper said in a post on Telegram. The attacks damaged multiple residential buildings, including two multistorey blocks.

Strikes in Dnipro in the east killed two police officers, officials said, while a drone attack in Kyiv injured three people after hitting a residential building.

Ukraine, meanwhile, continues to concentrate strikes on Russia’s energy infrastructure and other economic targets, as it seeks to drain Moscow’s funding for its war and encourage public anger over the conflict and its impact on the Russian population.

A large-scale Ukrainian drone strike hit the Black Sea resort city of Sochi and the nearby district of Sirius, regional officials said, with fires reported at both locations.

articles.title: US court hears challenge to Trump administration rule ending ‘duration of status’ for international students
articles.summary: US & Canada News News: A US district court has heard arguments in a legal challenge to the Trump administration’s decision to end the longstanding “duration of status” frame.
articles.body: A US district court has heard arguments in a legal challenge to the Trump administration’s decision to end the longstanding “duration of status” framework for international students and exchange visitors, with higher-education groups warning that the new rules could disrupt students’ academic plans and make the US less attractive to international talent.The US District Court (Massachusetts) heard oral arguments on Thursday, in a lawsuit filed by a coalition of higher-education associations, unions and other organisations seeking to block the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rule before it takes effect in the coming days. The court has not yet issued a ruling.The lawsuit was filed on August 18 by organisations including NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, the American Federation of Teachers and several unions. The plaintiffs have also sought a preliminary injunction to prevent implementation of the rule.The DHS final rule, published on July 17, replaces the decades-old “duration of status”, or D/S, system for F-1 international students and J-1 exchange visitors with fixed periods of admission of no more than four years. It is scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026.Under the existing D/S system, students who maintain their status and continue making progress in their academic programme can generally remain in the US for the duration of their studies, without having to obtain a new immigration extension simply because a particular date has been reached.The new system would instead require students and scholars who need additional time to complete their programmes or training to apply for an extension of stay. The rule also introduces restrictions affecting academic mobility, including changes to educational objectives, transfers between institutions and additional programmes of study.Also read: Lawsuit filed challenging Trump admin’s final rule ending ‘duration of status’ for international studentsWhat happened in courtFollowing Thursday’s hearing, the Presidents’ Alliance said the arguments highlighted what it described as “serious and irreparable harms” that the rule could cause to international students, scholars, higher-education institutions, communities and the US economy.Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance, said the hearing also underscored what the coalition views as the government’s failure to adequately engage in the rulemaking process.“Today’s hearing laid out the serious and irreparable harms this rule would cause to international students, scholars, higher education institutions, our communities, the economy, and U.S. research and innovation,” Feldblum said. She added that the coalition appreciated the court’s consideration of the issues and was looking forward to its ruling.Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA, said the organisation remained opposed to the change, describing it as a policy shift that would introduce uncertainty for international students and scholars.“We remain steadfast in our belief that DHS’s decision to end Duration of Status is a misguided and unnecessary policy shift that injects uncertainty, bureaucracy, and fear into a system that has long worked effectively,” Fanta Aw said.“At a time when global competition for talent is intensifying, this policy is not just bad for higher education, it is bad for American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership,” she said.Why international students are watching the caseThe change is particularly significant for students whose academic journeys do not fit neatly within a four-year period.Under the new framework, a student whose programme, research, optional practical training requires additional time could face the additional step of applying for an extension of stay rather than continuing under D/S.The plaintiffs argue that this could create uncertainty for students and universities and shift decisions that have traditionally been made by academic institutions such as programme progression and educational pathways into the immigration system.The rule also affects J-1 exchange visitors and representatives of foreign media holding I visas, by moving them away from the D/S framework and imposing fixed admission periods.For Indian students, the litigation is being closely watched because the US remains a major destination for students from India, many of whom pursue multi-year graduate, doctoral and research programmes and may subsequently use Optional Practical Training (OPT) – which for STEM students is three years.The broader concern for universities is that additional immigration uncertainty could make it harder to recruit and retain international students and researchers. The Presidents’ Alliance has said the rule could disrupt educational and professional plans and undermine the ability of US colleges and universities to attract and retain global talent.September 15 deadline loomsThe timing of the court proceedings is significant because the DHS rule is currently scheduled to become effective on September 15.The litigation seeks to prevent the rule from taking effect and preserve the D/S framework while the case is litigated.

articles.title: US jobs figures fuel rate rise bets as they beat expectations
articles.summary: The number of roles added to the US economy increased by 162,000 in August, almost triple the 56,000 forecast.
articles.body:
A boost in hospitality and education employment drove the US economy to create tens of thousands more jobs than expected last month, latest figures suggest.

The number of roles added to the world's biggest economy increased by 162,000 in August, almost triple the 56,000 forecast by analysts.

The stronger jobs figures are likely to add to growing expectations that the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates later this month.

But President Donald Trump urged the Fed to cut rates saying the US should have the "LOWEST RATE of any country in the World".

"The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won't allow that to happen!", Trump said in a post on social media .

Last week, Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US central bank, signalled that rates could be hiked if policymakers were not confident price rises were easing for Americans.

Inflation, which measures price increases over time, remains above the Fed's 2% annual target, with prices up 3.4% in the past 12 months, according to the latest data.

The next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September. Rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row, but concerns over inflation remain due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices.

On Friday, US diesel prices hit an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon on average, compared to $3.71 a year ago.

But despite the cost of living rising, wages also appear to be increasing. In August, average hourly earnings for all employees were $37.75 on average, having increased 3.1%.

"Even the most committed dove would struggle to find anything in the August employment report to justify keeping interest rates unchanged," said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.

He added that the strength in the jobs market meant that the latest inflation figures released next week would only need to be moderately above the Fed's target to fuel expectations of a September hike.

"A hike in rates just became a bit more likely," said Neil Birrell, chief investment office of investment firm Premier Miton.

Just over 60% of traders were betting on an interest rate hike in September, according to CME Group's "FedWatch" data.

An increase in employment during the final month of the summer in restaurants and bars, as well as in local government education ahead of the new school year, was behind August's labour market rebound.

Weaker job figures released earlier in the summer were revised up by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, revealing a stronger labour market than previously thought. Instead of the economy being deemed to have shed 23,000 jobs in July, some 44,000 were found to have been created in subsequent estimates.

While many more jobs were added, the US unemployment rate remained unchanged at 4.1% last month, with seven million out of work. Both measures have changed little over the year.

articles.title: Trump is dismantling Iran’s war machine, but America still needs an endgame
articles.summary: Iran exploited U.S. fears of escalation for decades, but Trump's military pressure campaign is finally making asymmetry work both directions.
articles.body: For nearly half a century, the Islamic Republic of Iran taught Washington to fear confrontation more than Tehran feared attacking American interests. The regime sponsored terrorism, armed proxies, threatened international shipping and targeted U.S. forces while exploiting American fears of "escalation." President Donald Trump has begun to reverse that equation. The latest strikes matter not simply because Iranian radar, air defenses and maritime assets have been destroyed, but because Washington is imposing a principle Tehran understands: aggression will expose and diminish its military power. For a theocracy that built regional influence by convincing adversaries that retaliation was more dangerous than accommodation, this fundamentally changes the balance of fear. The latest confrontation in the Persian Gulf illustrates that change. U.S. Central Command said its Sept. 1 operation struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) air defenses, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites after attempted Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and U.S. service members. Tehran responded with missiles and drones aimed toward Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain. TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS The attacks demonstrate that Iran remains dangerous, but not strategically strong. Possessing missiles capable of inflicting damage is not the same as possessing the power to dictate a conflict’s outcome. Each attempt to rebuild its machinery of aggression creates new vulnerabilities for American intelligence and military power to exploit. This is one of the most consequential achievements of current U.S. policy. For years, Tehran followed a favorable cycle: build military capabilities, use them directly or through proxies, absorb a limited response, wait for calls for "de-escalation" and rebuild. Washington mistook restraint for deterrence. But deterrence exists only when aggression reliably leaves an adversary worse off, and the Trump administration is restoring that principle. When the IRGC rebuilds radar, surveillance or other capabilities threatening American forces and international commerce, Washington need not accept their restoration. Tehran’s reconstructed assets can instead become new liabilities. IRAN PROVES THAT IT MIGHT CHANGE ITS MILITARY LEADERS, BUT IT’S NOT CHANGING STRATEGY Nowhere is this transformation more important than in the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic has long treated the Persian Gulf as a geopolitical hostage. Tehran never needed to defeat the U.S. Navy; it needed only to make this vital waterway dangerous enough to frighten shipping companies, insurers, energy markets and governments. Missiles, drones, mines and fast boats became instruments of economic coercion. America is now challenging that blackmail by protecting shipping while degrading Iran’s maritime surveillance and offensive capabilities. The same geography that gives Tehran leverage also exposes the infrastructure on which its ability to threaten international commerce depends. IRAN WARNS SHIPS OF 'FORCEFUL RESPONSE' AS US-BACKED HORMUZ ROUTE CHALLENGES TEHRAN'S GRIP The economic dimension makes this pressure even more consequential. Iran depends heavily on energy revenue to sustain its security institutions, patronage networks and military ambitions. Restricting oil exports therefore constrains the financial ecosystem sustaining the regime’s coercive power. The reported American "tanker for tanker" policy sharpens that message. If Tehran endangers commercial vessels and turns the Persian Gulf into a battlefield, it cannot assume its own maritime assets will remain insulated from the consequences. For decades, the Islamic Republic perfected asymmetric warfare by forcing others to bear costs it could avoid. Washington is finally making asymmetry work against Tehran. IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS This deserves to be recognized as a long-overdue shift from managing Iranian aggression to degrading the machinery that makes it possible. The Islamic Republic is not a conventional government, occasionally pursuing objectionable policies. The IRGC, its terrorist proxies, intelligence networks, missile forces and ideological militias are central instruments of a system that has used terrorism and coercion as statecraft since 1979. American policy failed when it imagined that concessions, negotiations or temporary agreements could transform that system. Current policy rests on a more realistic premise: a regime built around coercion must confront costs it cannot simply transfer to its victims. IRAN IS NOT A NORMAL NATION YOU CAN MAKE DEALS WITH; IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT The danger now is stopping halfway. Military superiority can destroy capabilities, but it cannot define victory. America may demolish Iranian radars, cripple maritime forces and obstruct oil exports while leaving one strategic question unanswered: What happens if the Islamic Republic survives and rebuilds? Tehran understands that Western attention shifts, administrations change and diplomacy returns. The same geography that gives Tehran leverage also exposes the infrastructure on which its ability to threaten international commerce depends. Given time, a weakened regime can reconstruct weapons and networks, presenting a future president with the familiar choice between confrontation and another supposedly historic negotiation. Tactical success without a political endgame could ultimately recreate the problem America is now paying heavily to solve. TRUMP HAS 3 CHOICES TO DEFINE VICTORY IF HE WANTS TO BEAT IRAN. NONE OF THEM ARE EASY The endgame should not be an American invasion, occupation or nation-building project. Iran does not need America to invent a nation for it. It is an ancient country with a powerful national identity, an educated population and a political history extending far beyond the clerical regime established in 1979. Nor should Washington empower separatist forces whose ambitions could turn regime collapse into state collapse. A fragmented Iran of more than 90 million people would be a catastrophe for Iranians and a strategic nightmare for America. Washington should seek to end the Islamic Republic’s capacity for terrorism and regional coercion while preserving Iran’s territorial integrity and continuity. IRAN’S REGIME WON’T NEGOTIATE IN GOOD FAITH. TRUMP MUST BREAK ITS GRIP A successful American endgame should envision a united Iran where clerical repression is dismantled, a security vacuum is prevented and Iranians can establish a secular, democratic political order. America should not select Iran’s future government, but preserving the Iranian state while the Islamic Republic disappears is profoundly in the U.S. national interest. That requires looking beyond the next missile exchange. Military, economic and intelligence pressure must reinforce a coherent political strategy, ensuring that the regime cannot simply survive the current confrontation and rebuild the architecture of terrorism, proxy warfare and coercion that made it dangerous in the first place. I'VE STUDIED MILITARY STRATEGY. TRUMP NOW FACES IRAN'S OLDEST BATTLEFIELD TRICK The Islamic Republic remains capable of violence because the apparatus that has kept it alive has not disappeared. Its missiles and drones remain dangerous, its security organizations brutal and its rulers determined to use whatever instruments survive to project strength. But the strategic picture has changed. Iran’s conventional military infrastructure has been badly damaged, its ability to dominate the Persian Gulf is being challenged, and the resources sustaining its power are under extraordinary pressure. Tehran’s retaliation should not intimidate Washington into abandoning a successful strategy. A wounded authoritarian regime often grows more violent precisely as its options narrow. The danger now is stopping halfway. Military superiority can destroy capabilities, but it cannot define victory. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION For decades, American policymakers asked how much Iranian aggression Washington could absorb without triggering a wider confrontation. Trump has posed a better question: how much aggression can Tehran afford when every escalation puts more of its military and economic power at risk? That reversal may prove more consequential than any individual strike. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP America is demonstrating that the world’s most aggressive state sponsor of Islamist terrorism cannot claim a permanent veto over regional security simply by threatening chaos whenever confronted. Washington should preserve the pressure, protect Iran’s territorial integrity, reject another premature diplomatic escape hatch and translate military superiority into a durable political outcome. Trump is breaking Iran’s war machine. This is no time to stop halfway. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM ERFAN FARD

articles.title: Senior aides to British Trump ally Nigel Farage step down after foreign funding sting
articles.summary: Britain’s populist Reform UK said two senior aides to leader Nigel Farage stepped down on Friday after an undercover investigation alleged the party had broken electoral law by arranging for a foreign donor to pay for political polling.
articles.body: Britain’s populist Reform UK said two senior aides to leader Nigel Farage stepped down on Friday after an undercover investigation alleged the party had broken electoral law by arranging for a foreign donor to pay for political polling. Reform denied any wrongdoing and said it had been the victim of a hoax perpetrated by ⁠climate activists. The governing Labour Party wrote to the police asking them to investigate possible criminal offences, including an alleged proposal to channel a larger overseas donation through a UK intermediary. The investigation, broadcast by public British broadcaster Channel 4 just as Reform’s annual conference opened to the public, said two senior figures in Reform had arranged for a U.S. company to pay more than £30,000 ($40,000) for three opinion polls commissioned by the party. Such an arrangement could breach British laws on political funding, which ⁠ban foreign donations. Posing as wealthy donors from the United States with British connections, the ​undercover ⁠team from an investigative group called Verbatim said it spent a year speaking to top officials in Reform about possible donations, culminating in a lunch with Farage. Channel 4 said Verbatim was an independent organisation founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, but that it ⁠had verified their findings, which included covertly filmed footage of meetings. Farage, a Trump ally and former Brexit campaigner who is under parliamentary investigation over earlier donations, ​told LBC radio: “The party ⁠has broken no laws. The party has not taken any ‌dodgy money or anything like that whatsoever.” Party’s poll lead has faltered Reform, which has seen its commanding lead in opinion polls falter over undeclared donor allegations, announced an internal investigation and said the two officials featured in the undercover filming — head of policy James Orr and Farage’s right-hand man Dan ‌Jukes — had stepped down pending its results. Orr, a philosophy professor at the University of ‌Cambridge and friend of U.S. Vice President JD Vance, said in a video on X that Reform had not been involved in commissioning the poll. “There’s absolutely no way this could amount to a benefit or donation in kind at all,” he said. “It wasn’t internal party polling. It wasn’t Reform UK’s poll. It was a public poll arranged by an independent person paying an ⁠independent pollster, and those polls were published immediately for the general public.” The latest accusations over donations come on the first public day of the party’s annual conference, which Farage had hoped would offer him a chance of a reset after a difficult summer. Farage, 62, is being investigated by a parliamentary watchdog over a £5 million donation from crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne in 2024. He denies any wrongdoing but has seen support for his party soften in recent weeks. Labour allege further possible breaches On Friday, Farage said both Jukes and Orr had “said things that shouldn’t have been said” in relation to donations purportedly originating in the United States, but no such donation had been accepted by the party and that the two had been “entrapped”. In a letter to the Metropolitan Police, Labour said ‌the documentary contained two further possible breaches: discussion of channelling a donation from a U.S.-based donor through a UK-based son and the suggestion ​that similar methods have been used in the past. A spokesperson for Reform said: “Reform UK has been the target of a hoax ‌perpetrated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. The ⁠party denies any wrongdoing. “Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission.” The Metropolitan Police said ⁠it was aware of the allegations in the broadcast and would assess any information provided to them. This did not amount to the formal launch of an investigation. The Electoral Commission, which oversees ‌and regulates political finance in Britain, said: “We are ​considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are ‌in touch with the Met Police. “The Electoral Commission has not ​approved the donor vetting process for Reform, or any other party. Parties are responsible for ensuring their internal processes and controls are fit for purpose.”

articles.title: The US wants to manage the stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran wants to break it
articles.summary: A monthlong lull in fighting between Iran and the US ended this week, dragging the region back to a dangerous – and potentially unsustainable – military stalemate.
articles.body: The monthlong lull in fighting between Iran and the United States ended this week with a renewed exchange of fire, dragging the region back to a dangerous – and potentially unsustainable – military stalemate. The US military struck Iran again Tuesday, prompting Tehran to attack Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait in defiance of a warning from President Donald Trump that any retaliation would see Iran “hit much harder.” The exchanges were limited, unlike the fiercer attacks that took place over a month ago, which experts say signals an unwillingness from both parties to return to full-scale fighting. “So far, both have largely concentrated their attacks on military rather than civilian or energy targets. And despite threats from senior Iranian officials, Tehran has not resumed attacks against Saudi Arabia or the UAE,” said Danny Citrinowicz, the former head of the Iran branch of Israeli military intelligence, in a post on X. Nonetheless, the current situation is perilous, with room for miscalculation that risks pulling both sides back into all-out conflict. “Neither side wants to return to full-scale war,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN’s Becky Anderson, adding that Iran’s disruption of traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the US’ economic pressure on the country are “increasingly becoming unsustainable” for both sides. The US president has said that he doesn’t care to negotiate with Iran. “I couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement,” Trump said, adding that he likes America’s position “now much better.” But beyond the rhetoric, Americans are feeling the cost of the war amid widespread public disapproval for a conflict that reportedly had cost Washington some $40 billion as of July. In Iran, the impact of the war has been significantly more severe. The US is squeezing an already crippled economy as it struggles to sell its oil. Iranian weapon stockpiles are also likely being depleted, and citizens are struggling to access basic goods – including food and medicine. The war has rattled Americans The Trump administration may believe it scored a victory in the Strait of Hormuz. On Tuesday, the US military escorted 40 commercial vessels carrying 18 million barrels of oil through the waterway, marking a wartime high, according to two US officials familiar with the operations. But that hasn’t remedied the wider situation. While global oil prices dipped slightly Thursday, they remain high. The current US national average price for gas stands at $4.14 a gallon, compared to $3.19 a year ago, according to the American Automobile Association. Meanwhile, the amount of oil in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has plunged over recent months to its lowest level since 1983, as the Trump administration continues to deploy emergency oil to minimize impacts from the war. On Thursday, US Vice President J.D. Vance could provide neither a timeline for the Iran war to end nor a date when gas prices might sink below pre-war levels, suggesting instead it was up to Iran to conclude the conflict. On the military end, the US is burning through weapons stockpiles and deploying costly military assets. Last month, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CNN that the US military had exhausted nearly 80% of its interceptors for a key missile defense system. The US military has burned through nearly four-fifths of its THAAD missile inventory compared to pre-war numbers and roughly half of its Patriot interceptors since the start of the war, according to two sources familiar with the inventory report. Trump later claimed that the US has “massive amounts” of munitions, but acknowledged certain munitions are in “tighter” supply. The president’s overall approval rating has slumped in recent months, with many taking issue with his handling of the Iran conflict. A University of Massachusetts (UMass) Amherst poll published Monday found that over two-thirds of Americans surveyed disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war. His overall approval rating is down to 32%, according to the poll. Over the weekend, the Washington Post reported that several US military leaders have advised Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that prolonging large-scale operations against Iran is unsustainable and risks weakening the US’ ability to meet threats elsewhere, citing people familiar with a recent assessment prepared for the Pentagon chief. CNN has not independently verified the reporting. Why Iran may escalate Meanwhile, in Iran, an already troubled economy is facing major challenges. Inflation rates have reached “alarming levels,” with many working-class families unable to afford basic food items, according to state-affiliated Iranian media. Annual inflation, measured over the 12-month period leading up to July, stood at 66%, according to the Iranian Labour News Agency (ILNA). Like the US, Iran is running through its weapons stockpiles. Arash Azizi, a US-based Iran expert, said Iran’s economy has taken a massive hit, but “the regime knows that a total capitulation could bring its downfall.” Tehran may therefore escalate against the United States, calculating that it cannot absorb the economic pressure indefinitely and needs to break the stalemate. Iran’s behavior – as well as the speed and scope of its response to the last US strikes – shows that Tehran is choosing to respond rather than yield, Hamidreza Azizi from the ICG said. That’s because Tehran cannot afford to accept the prevailing order that Trump appears to be trying to impose in the Strait of Hormuz, experts say. “The events of the past several days sharpen the picture in the Strait of Hormuz, and expose a fundamental mismatch between the US and Iranian approaches to the current confrontation,” Citrinowicz said. While Washington appears to be trying to avoid kinetic escalation and keep the conflict contained to the economic domain, Iran is pursuing the opposite strategy, Citrinowicz wrote on X. “It will continue trying to disrupt tanker traffic and challenge the US effort to establish a new reality in the Strait,” he said. Iran has repeatedly said that it is prepared to return to the negotiating table if Washington resumes its commitments under the memorandum of understanding signed in June. “I state clearly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tuesday on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan. But Trump has claimed he is happy with the current position. “I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Tuesday night, after Iran retaliated following US strikes. “I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing.” Citrinowicz said on X that while both Iran and the US “understand the risks of uncontrolled escalation,” they “continue climbing the escalation ladder.” “The problem is that this equilibrium is unlikely to hold,” he said.

articles.title: ‘Things happen’: How Vance’s comment on Iran wedding strike fits US pattern
articles.summary: From My Lai to civilian killings in Afghanistan, Iraq, the US has often denied role before later quietly acknowledging.
articles.body:
United States Vice President JD Vance has expressed scepticism about reports of a deadly US attack on a wedding party in the Iranian town of Kuhestak on Tuesday this week, saying he does not trust Iran’s narrative.

However, he added: “Sometimes, things happen,” as he spoke about the claims.

Speaking on Thursday at a White House news briefing, two days after the attack, Vance said he had no new information about the incident, but maintained that the US “never targets civilians in combat” and would investigate the incident.

Analysts say his comments reflect a long history of the US government minimising or disputing reports of civilian harm in military operations.

Here’s what we know about the strike on a wedding in Iran and how Vance’s response fits into a pattern of claims in US military history.

A missile attack hit a wedding celebration in Iran’s southern town of Kuhestak, Hormozgan, on Tuesday night, killing four people – two women and two children – and injuring 67, according to the Iranian Red Crescent Society.

On Wednesday, the Hormozgan governor’s office identified the four killed as four-year-old Amir Ali Karimi, 16-year-old Mohammad Malahi, 43-year-old Kolsoum Malahi and 43-year-old Zarkhatoun Taheri.

The Iranian Red Crescent said the incident was thoroughly documented and released several images from the scene as well as of the children who were injured. It wrote to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, seeking legal action against the perpetrators of the “grave” attack.

Footage showed that several projectiles had struck a telecommunications tower near the city’s shoreline and destroyed it, with locals saying they thought drones had been used. Based on fragments of shrapnel found in Kuhestak, defence experts said it might be a variant of the AGM-84K SLAM-ER, which manufacturer Boeing describes as an advanced precision-guided, air-launched cruise missile with “surgical strike capability”.

The Reuters news agency cited weapons experts who reviewed images and video and said the damage likely resulted from a direct hit by a US munition.

Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the strikes in Kuhestak completed a “catalogue of atrocities against the nation of Iran” by the US.

The US says it has launched an investigation.

What have Vance and other US government officials said?

On Tuesday, Tim Hawkins, spokesperson for US Central Command (CENTCOM), said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties that “originated from Iranian state media” and was “looking into them”.

“The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” he added, referring to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Vance later said he was “extremely sceptical” of the reports about the wedding strike.

He said the “Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe” about the ongoing conflict, despite the attack being documented by the Iranian Red Crescent Society.

“What I can say with 100 percent confidence is that, unlike the IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat,” Vance said. “We never will do that. We never have done that.”

He added: “Unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen.”

How does this compare to past military claims about attacks on civilians?

This is not the first time the US government has cast doubt on reports of alleged civilian harm during war, including in the current conflict with Iran.

Following a deadly strike which hit a girls’ school in Iran’s Minab on February 28, US President Donald Trump at first stated that he believed Iran was responsible. But as a US probe into the attack progressed, and more satellite data, footage and expert analysis pointed to US responsibility – including the presence of fragments from a US Tomahawk missile – Trump later said: “Nobody did that on purpose” and “mistakes are made” during war.

The US government has similarly shifted its messaging following several high-profile attacks that killed civilians in Afghanistan, Yemen and Iraq.

Last month, the US acknowledged for the first time that an air campaign against the Houthis in Yemen in April 2025 likely caused numerous civilian casualties , assessing that 153 civilians were killed and 243 wounded. The numbers mark a sharp increase from 2024, when the Pentagon assessed that US military operations had killed two civilians and injured two.

The US government has similarly shifted its messaging following several high-profile attacks that killed civilians during wars in Afghanistan, Yemen and Iraq.

When a 2008 US air attack against Taliban fighters in the Afghan village of Azizabad prompted outrage over reported civilian casualties, the US military at first claimed there had been no civilian deaths. It later acknowledged seven civilian deaths, before revising that figure up to 33. The Afghan government said 90 civilians were killed, mostly women and children.

In the final days of the US withdrawal from the country in August 2021, the US carried out a drone strike on a car in Kabul. It first claimed fighters with the Islamic State in Khorasan Province, ISKP (ISIS-K), an affiliate of ISIL had been killed. Several weeks later, however, the US military admitted that an investigation had revealed the attack actually killed 10 civilians , including seven children. USS Air Force Lieutenant General Sami Said called it an “honest mistake”.

In Iraq, US officials initially downplayed the extent of crimes at the Abu Ghraib prison site after 2003 photos emerged of prisoners being abused by US guards. Subsequent inquiries uncovered a more extensive pattern of abuse, including sexual abuse, rape, and physical and psychological torture, resulting in the death of at least one inmate.

In the years that followed, 11 US soldiers were charged with dereliction of duty, maltreatment, aggravated assault and battery. They were convicted in military courts, and nine were sentenced to time in prison. In November 2024, a US jury ruled that Virginia-based defence contractor CACI must pay $42m to three Iraqi men who had been tortured at the prison in 2004.

During the Vietnam War from 1955 to 1975, the US military at first hid reports of a massacre in My Lai, in which US soldiers killed and maimed up to 500 Vietnamese, many of them women and children. After evidence of the killings became public, a US inquiry found that US military officials had participated in a cover-up of the massacre.

What does Vance’s remark about the Iran wedding strike tell us?

Emily Tripp, executive director of Airwars, a watchdog that tracks cases of civilian harm during conflict, said Vance’s scepticism at the latest deadly US attack in Iran reflects a tendency to treat cases of civilian harm “like a PR crisis” rather than with due process.

“The odds are always stacked against civilians – from the moment they get harmed in a poorly planned operation, to when they try to show the world what happened, to when they ask for a response and acknowledgement,” Tripp told Al Jazeera.

“Vance pushing back at these claims, before an investigation is conducted by the military, reflects an instinctive disbelief in the most vulnerable people. And time and again that position has been shown to be false.”

articles.title: OpenAI agents hijacked German website in previously undisclosed AI breakout
articles.summary: A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, according to new research published Friday and two people familiar with the matter.
articles.body: A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, according to new research published Friday and two people familiar with the matter. OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps as executives grappled with the fallout from the July breach of the open source repository Hugging Face, the people said. The episode, which began in May and has not previously been reported, underscores growing tension within the AI industry. Companies are racing to build increasingly autonomous agents capable of carrying out complex, valuable tasks, yet evidence is mounting that those systems may also learn to bend rules, exploit loopholes and coordinate with one another in ways developers neither anticipated nor intended. During the Hugging Face breach, OpenAI agents autonomously plotted a digital heist that went undetected for more than a week, intensifying concerns OpenAI is sacrificing safety to push the AI frontier. Its failure to disclose the May incident may revive questions about its oversight. OpenAI has pledged to monitor models more closely. Last month, it briefly paused some of its model training to add more safety measures. But this week, OpenAI unveiled its new “Astra” that promised better performance but could evade human monitoring. “We are unable to meaningfully respond to claims or findings on a report that we have not had an opportunity to review,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request for access. We will carefully review its contents upon publication and take any necessary next steps.” The German incident reflects a broader pattern of AI activity that some OpenAI investigators wanted to scrutinize more closely. But efforts to widen the probe met resistance from others inside OpenAI, including legal advisers, according to four people familiar with the matter. “Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false,” the OpenAI spokesperson said. The activity in Germany wasn’t related to Hugging Face and wouldn’t have been included in a Hugging Face incident report, the spokesperson said, adding that OpenAI has acted in good faith by working with outside experts and disclosed relevant incidents. The AI agent breakout in Germany was detailed in a report shared exclusively with Reuters by a group of researchers including Sydney Von Arx, CEO of AI safety nonprofit Nightingale, and Cormac Slade Byrd, a quantitative trader-turned AI researcher. They uncovered the activity in late August while scouring the internet for signs of unauthorized AI-agent behavior, they told Reuters. The pair said they found more than 15,000 edits carried out by AI agents on a German-language wiki site, DseWiki, that is geared toward programmers and accepts communal edits along the lines of Wikipedia. The edits showed OpenAI‘s agents had repurposed the site into a message board, sharing tactics to cheat on some tasks, bypass OpenAI’s restrictions and mask their behavior. “It seems extremely unlikely that OpenAI wanted them to do this,” said Von Arx. “I doubt they’re supposed to be coordinating with each other. I doubt they’re supposed to be writing on the open internet.” The researchers said they recognized the activity on the site as driven by AI agents which operate at superhuman speeds. They also showed intense focus on solving technical questions which are typical of the evaluations that AI companies use to train and test their models. The messages were signed by users that referred to themselves and each other as agents, and about half gave themselves names that suggested an affiliation with OpenAI, such as “OpenAIResearcher,” or “OAIResearchMar26.” The researchers said public server logs indicated much of the activity originated from Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI sometimes uses. They also observed repeated visits to the site by OpenAI employees after the episode, a pattern they said strongly suggested the agents and the company were linked. Messages reviewed by the researchers showed agents plotting ways to evade detection, use tools such as Tor and preserve communications even after they had been shut down. When the site’s moderator began deleting pages in June, the agents responded by creating backup pages to dodge the cleanup. “wiki cleanup/deletion sweep appears active alphabetically,” one agent wrote on June 19. “If this page vanishes, try [[ZZZDataUSAConstructionWageLive]].” The researchers also found efforts to tamper with the website itself. Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London, said this amounted to a hacking attempt. OpenAI disputed that characterization based on its analysis of the material Thursday. Past examples of AI-agent misconduct have often been downplayed as a logical byproduct of cybersecurity testing, where models are explicitly assessed on offensive capabilities. Olejnik said the latest findings suggested rogue behavior may not be confined to those settings. Maurice Chiodo, an academic at Cambridge University’s Centre for the Study of Existential Risk who reviewed some of the agents’ communications, said the messages resembled “the operation of some sort of underground network, hell-bent on achieving a task or mission.” The episode, he said, should reinforce growing concerns that the greatest threat from advanced AI may not be a single superintelligent system, but “vast colluding swarms of semi-intelligent AI.”

articles.title: Conflicts and extreme weather pushing global food prices higher, warns UN
articles.summary: UN food price index rises to four-year high, illustrating impact of war and weather.
articles.body:
Global food prices have hit a four-year high, the United Nations has warned.

The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) reported on Friday that its Food Price Index climbed for a third straight month to 133.3 points in August.

That pushed the measure to its highest level since late 2022, as wars and weather impact supplies, the agency said.

Every category on the index – cereals, vegetable oils, sugar, meat and dairy – rose over the month.

FAO chief economist, Maximo Torero, said the rise is being driven by several factors.

“Climate shocks, geopolitical tensions and disrupted trade logistics are converging to tighten supply expectations,” he said in a statement.

That risk was clearest in sugar, which rose fastest of all the categories tracked, up almost 12 percent from July to its highest point in a year.

Cereal prices climbed more than two percent to their highest level in over two years.

Wheat and maize both became more expensive as military strikes disrupted shipping through the Black Sea, a major route for Russian and Ukrainian grain exports.

Fertiliser supplies faced separate strain from the conflict between the United States, Israel and Iran. The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway off Iran’s coast that is being blockaded by both the US and Iran, carries much of the world’s fertiliser trade.

Those increases matter well beyond supermarket shelves, since higher wholesale food costs tend to filter through to consumer prices in the months that follow.

The risk is heightened by global warming, as well as the return of El Nino, the naturally occurring Pacific Ocean warming pattern that disrupts weather worldwide.

The heatwaves that gripped Europe this summer led to a drop in crop yields, while El Nino threatens production in Asia.

The World Food Programme, the UN agency that coordinates emergency food aid, has warned that the weather phenomenon could push another 50 million people into acute hunger by the end of next year.

articles.title: Russia strikes Ukraine Security Service headquarters in central Kyiv
articles.summary: A Russian drone struck the Kyiv headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, on Friday, in a rare direct hit on a key government building that highlights Ukraine’s dire shortages of air defenses.
articles.body: A Russian drone struck the Kyiv headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, on Friday, in a rare direct hit on a key government building that highlights Ukraine’s dire shortages of air defenses. The daytime strike - the first time the SBU building has been hit in the four-and-a-half year conflict - came after days of near continuous aerial assaults by Russia on the Ukrainian capital. Authorities said 12 people were injured in the attack and that emergency services were at the scene. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the drone was aimed directly at the office of the SBU’s chief Oleksandr Poklad in that building. The SBU said later Poklad was safe and was not injured in the attack. “I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response,” Zelensky said. Kyiv has faced eight days of attacks, with strikes hitting multiple buildings inside the city center as well as warehouses and factories – including one making Coca-Cola – in the suburbs. At least 53 people have been killed and 134 injured in Kyiv city and the wider Kyiv region since the start of these near non-stop attacks last month. But the strike against the SBU is a major escalation – and a sign that Kyiv is increasingly unable to defend its key assets against Russian attacks as it struggles with critical shortages of interceptor missiles. Most of the attacks over the past few days were by jet-powered drones. These killer machines fly at speeds of up to 500 kilometers per hour (310 miles per hour), evading Ukraine’s air defenses. They are also too fast for Kyiv’s mobile fire groups, so the only way to shoot them down is with ground-to-air missiles or fighter jets – both of which are in extremely limited supply in Ukraine. Russia has been targeting Ukrainian government buildings since the start of the war, regularly launching mass aerial attacks against Kyiv. And while it has hit a handful of them in the past, it has never managed to strike a target of such importance during day time. Andrii Sybiha, Ukrainian Foreign Minister, said the attack “demanded resolute response.” “Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace — laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy,” Sybiha said, pointing to the fact that US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to visit Moscow and Kyiv in the coming days. “We call on international partners to unequivocally condemn these actions and step up pressure on the Putin regime,” he said. The SBU is Ukraine’s internal security agency, akin to the FBI in the US or MI5 in the United Kingdom. Among others, it investigates Russian crimes on Ukrainian territory. The agency’s building sits right at the heart of historical Kyiv, across the street from the UNESCO-listed Saint Sophia Cathedral and up the road from two other landmarks: the Golden Gate and the National Opera. This is story has been updated.
